Democratic Senator Abdul El-Sayed reacts after his victory in the US midterm elections, in Detroit, Michigan, United States [File: Brian Snyder/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has launched a political action committee called “Habibi PAC”, days after becoming the first Muslim member of the United States Senate.
Political action committees, or PACs, are organisations that raise and spend money to support or oppose candidates for office.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3‘Call me senator’: How Abdul El-Sayed beat Trump’s hate to create historylist 2 of 3The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 US midtermslist 3 of 3Abdul El-Sayed did not have to become less Muslim to winend of list
A Federal Election Commission filing dated on Thursday shows that Habibi PAC is registered as a leadership PAC sponsored by El-Sayed. Such committees are separate from a politician’s own campaign.
Habibi, an Arabic term of endearment meaning “my dear” or “my beloved”, is a word El-Sayed used often on the campaign trail, including in his victory speech in Detroit, when he addressed Vice President JD Vance directly: “JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January.”
He is one of several newly elected Democrats to register leadership PACs since Tuesday’s vote, according to FEC filings. They include Arizona Congressman-elect Amish Shah’s “PACStreet Boy”, Iowa Senator-elect Josh Turek’s “WheelPAC” and North Carolina Senator-elect Roy Cooper’s “One NC PAC”.

Doncic has scored at least 40 points in six of his last seven games and joined Elgin Baylor, Kobe Bryant and George Mikan as the only Lakers players to score 40 or more in four straight regular-season contests.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire [File: Kirby Lee/US Today Sports]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
The mayor of Houston, the most populous city in the US state of Texas, has ordered the city’s police force to sharply limit its cooperation with the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
John Whitmire’s executive order came on Friday, days after Democrats swept statewide offices in the traditionally Republican state.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Can America ever return to pre-Trump politics?list 2 of 3Republicans redrew this Texas district to win – it narrowly workedlist 3 of 3How the US midterm elections reflected resistance to data centresend of list
According to the order, Houston police will contact ICE only when a person is being arrested for a jailable offence, according to the Reuters news agency.
Whitmire said he had consulted Texas’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller before acting, and that the move was meant to reduce fear and anxiety across the city.
“Elections matter,” Whitmire told reporters. “I do this to begin a healing process,” he said, adding he hoped his executive order would become a model for other Texas cities.
Joining Whitmire at the news conference, Houston Police ⁠Chief J Noe Diaz said he supported the change and that his department had already begun to implement the new policy.
Under the new rules, people stopped for minor traffic violations will no longer be referred to ICE simply because they have an administrative immigration warrant.
The decision reverses a policy Whitmire put in place in April under pressure from outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott.

Mustapha Harmouch, 33, says he learns something new every time he goes metal detecting [Hajar Elkahlaoui/Al Jazeera]By Hajar ElkahlaouiPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Agadir, Morocco – Mustapha Harmouch moves slowly across the sand at Agadir’s Corniche, sweeping his metal detector in low, even arcs. He tunes out the surfers paddling beyond the shore, the children shrieking in the waves and the chatter of families, all his attention is on one sound: the beep that means the coil has passed over something buried beneath the sand.
For the 33-year-old content creator, that uncertainty is the whole appeal. The detector does not distinguish between treasure and rubbish, it gives the same signal whether the object below is a coin, a ring, a discarded piece of aluminium, or an old piece of fishing equipment.
“The excitement comes partly from not knowing what lies beneath the sand,” he told Al Jazeera English.
Harmouch bought a Tianxun TX 850 metal detector online about four years ago. What began as a hobby has since become an occasional part of the videos he posts on Stofishing, a YouTube travel and spearfishing channel with roughly 123,000 subscribers.The search can stretch for hours, with every sweep of the detector offering the possibility of an unexpected find [Hajar Elkahlaoui/Al Jazeera]
“It’s a nice hobby because it’s the kind of exploration where I find something and learn something new,” he said. “Each outing is a chance to encounter something I would otherwise never have known about.”
That curiosity has led him to old coins, including some associated with historical periods and places such as the Al Haouz region and Fez.

item.title: Do not investigate Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office
item.description:
By Ziyad Motala
Professor of law at Howard University School of Law.Published On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026Listen

A hat reading 'VETO' sits on the Resolute Desk as US President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington on November 5, 2026 [AFP]
In a functioning constitutional democracy, allegations of corporate corruption would ordinarily invite immediate investigation. Congress would demand documents, summon executives and expose wrongdoing to public scrutiny.
With Democrats having won control of both houses of Congress, the expectation will be that they exercise these oversight powers vigorously. In Donald Trump’s America, however, there is a compelling argument for doing precisely the opposite.
If the objective is criminal accountability rather than political theatre, the incoming Democratic majorities might be better advised to preserve the evidence but postpone public congressional investigations and disclosures concerning potential criminal wrongdoing by Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office in January 2029, thereby avoiding the possibility of presidential pardons that could place those responsible beyond the reach of federal criminal prosecution.
This may sound absurd, but it follows from the extraordinary breadth of the presidential pardon power. Under the US Constitution, a president may pardon individuals for federal crimes before they have been charged, investigated or convicted. What was conceived as an exceptional power of mercy can become an instrument for protecting political associates, wealthy benefactors and corporate executives from criminal accountability.
